comparator.name: Scandinavian Languages and Cultures
comparator.sourceNotes: The ordinary full-time Scandinavia Studies pathway has 60 EC per year. Danish is retained as the first-listed main-language choice independently of UCR fit. This illustration selects Copenhagen from the detailed exchange course’s first compatible destination. The 30 EC exchange follows the regional cultural-history, language/translation and literature subject lines; main Scandinavian language-proficiency courses are excluded from that block. The 30 EC third-year free-choice group is separate. The 12 EC graduation project retains its prior-credit and writing-language rules. A home alternative requires Examination Board approval and is not stacked. Diagnostic and tutoring requirements carry no credits.
components: The first year also requires a Dutch writing diagnostic. Tutoring and study guidance continue throughout the programme. These requirements carry no credits.
The Human World: Introduction to the Humanities
A World of Regions: Introduction to Area Studies
From Yggdrasil to Urban Slang: Languages of the North
Attend Danish 1–3 before this course. The Vikings course then requires attendance in Danish 1–4 and Modern Scandinavia.
Danish Language Proficiency 1 and Modern Denmark
This example uses Danish as the main language. Norwegian and Swedish are alternative main-language choices.
Danish Language Proficiency 2 and Modern Denmark
Danish Language Proficiency 3: Danish Culture, History and Society A
Complete Danish 2 before Danish 3. The language sequence also develops knowledge of Danish history, culture and contemporary society.
Danish Language Proficiency 4: Danish Culture, History and Society B
Complete the first-year Danish route before this course. It studies nineteenth- to twenty-first-century poetry, fiction and other literary texts in Danish.
Danish Language Proficiency 5 and Receptive Norwegian and Swedish
Pass Danish 4 before Danish 5. This unit also develops reading and listening in Norwegian and Swedish.
Philosophy of Science: National Identity, Borders and Territory

This example uses Copenhagen, the first Danish destination in the exchange course list. Complete at least 54 first-year EC and attend the first semester of year two before departure. The 30 EC must follow programme subject lines in cultural history, language/translation or literature; Danish, Norwegian and Swedish language-proficiency courses cannot count. A home alternative requires Examination Board approval.
Complete the earlier language preparation, including Danish 5 and receptive-language study, and Languages of the North before this research project.
Complete Danish 1–5 before translation. The course combines Danish-to-Dutch practice, source-text analysis, translation theory and Danish creative writing.

Use this 30 EC for electives, a minor, a placement or approved study abroad. Normally no more than 12 EC may be introductory; an approved UvA minor or same-language sequence can permit up to 24 EC. External study needs Examination Board approval. Placements can occupy at most 12 EC, and minors must not duplicate the required language study.

Complete the first year and at least 54 second-year EC before starting the thesis. A January workshop develops the proposal. The thesis is 8,000–10,000 words on a Scandinavian regional, linguistic, literary or cultural topic within available supervisory expertise. It is written in a Scandinavian language if assessed writing proficiency reaches B2/C1 or above; otherwise it is written in Dutch.

routeSelection.basis: Danish is first in the current dated language-path list and remains the complete retained main-language choice, independent of UCR comparability. Copenhagen is the first Danish-compatible destination in the detailed exchange course list; no other main-language pathway or exchange destination is stacked.

exception.reason: UCR offers related study in literature, comparative myth, language processing, cultural interpretation, European institutions, social policy and research methods. These contributions do not form sustained study of Scandinavia’s languages, literatures, cultural histories or contemporary societies across a full programme. The wider combinations become general humanities or European social science rather than a sufficiently close response to Scandinavia Studies.

exception.ucrCourseEvidence: Three complete 24-course trials passed current offering, prerequisite and numerical checks. All 151 active identities were screened and plausible regional, literary, language, social and policy content was considered. Norse myth, psycholinguistics, stylistic analysis, cultural/Indigenous history, welfare economics and European institutions receive full consideration. Their documented contributions do not sustain the region-centred academic substance. The conclusion does not rest on a degree title, language acquisition alone, professional qualification, planning gaps or a quota of Nordic courses.

candidateAssessment.concept: Scandinavian language, linguistics and cultural inquiry
candidateAssessment.assessment: The closest trial combines literary interpretation, psycholinguistics, stylistics, rhetoric, creative communication, media, qualitative inquiry and social theory. Psycholinguistics substantively studies language acquisition, processing, bilingualism and experiments; Style and Meaning teaches grammar/discourse/cognition in interpretation. Comparative myth includes Norse material. The combination supports broad language-and-culture inquiry, but does not sustain Scandinavian linguistic relationships, cultural source study or the region’s societies and literatures. Missing language acquisition alone is not the decision criterion.

candidateAssessment.concept: Scandinavian literature, cultural history and Nordic identity
candidateAssessment.assessment: The second trial tests the complete literature sequence, myth, media/film/documentary, art interpretation, comparative histories, identity theory and qualitative research. These provide substantial methods and cultural-historical inquiry; Norse myth is an actual regional bridge. The history and media courses have their documented American, Indigenous or global settings, and art/heritage study supplies particular non-Nordic settings. Their combined teaching does not accumulate into Scandinavian literary history, northern cultural memory or regional identity research.

candidateAssessment.concept: Nordic societies, politics and northern-European history
candidateAssessment.assessment: The third trial tests comparative politics, EU institutions and law, international relations, policy, public economics, public health, modern/imperial history, sociology and research methods. Welfare, redistribution, democratic institutions and civil society provide genuine academic responses to interests in social systems. The composition does not establish sustained teaching of Nordic institutions, welfare-model development, regional modern history or the North/Arctic and Indigenous issues that organise the target. The current evidence does not justify carrying forward the old brief-Sweden-example claim as a regional curriculum.

audience.programmeDescription: Scandinavian Languages and Cultures at the University of Amsterdam, presented as Scandinavia Studies, examines the region’s languages, literature, cultural history and contemporary societies. Students specialise in Danish, Norwegian or Swedish and develop receptive knowledge of the other two languages. This example follows Danish and includes study in Copenhagen.
